steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a conceptual, step-by-step picture of how a Transformer works. Think of it as a modular recipe that repeatedly lets every token “ask” about every other token, then refines those interactions:

1. Input Representation  
   • Tokenization: split text into tokens (words, subwords, etc.).  
   • Embedding: map each token to a dense vector (e.g. 512- or 1024-dimensional).  
   • Positional Encoding: since embeddings alone have no notion of order, add a vector encoding “position in the sequence” (sinusoidal or learned) to each token embedding.

2. The Encoder (if you’re doing an encoder–decoder task like translation)  
   The encoder is a stack of N identical layers. Each layer has two sub-modules:  
     a. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
     b. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)  

   Between sub-modules you always have:  
     – A residual (skip) connection: you add the sub-module’s input to its output.  
     – Layer normalization: you normalize the summed result for stability.

   2.1 Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA)  
     • Purpose: let each token “look at” every other token and decide how much to pay attention to it.  
     • Mechanism, per head:  
       – Project each token’s embedding into three vectors: a Query (Q), a Key (K), and a Value (V).  
       – For token i and token j compute score(i,j) = Q_i · K_j / √d_k.  
       – Softmax over j to turn scores into attention weights.  
       – Weighted sum of V’s gives a context vector for token i.  
     • Multi-head: do this in parallel H times with different projections, then concatenate the H context vectors and linearly project back to model dimension.  
     • Intuition: each head can focus on a different kind of relationship (syntax, coreference, topic, etc.).

   2.2 Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
     • A simple two-layer MLP applied independently to each position:  
         FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1) W2 + b2  
     • Expands dimension then projects back, giving the model more representational power.

   2.3 Stacking  
     • You stack L such layers.  
     • Early layers learn basic relationships, later layers build more abstract, task-specific features.

3. The Decoder (for generation)  
   Also an L-layer stack, but each layer has three sub-modules:  
     1. Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention  
       – Same as above, but you mask future positions so that the model can’t “peek ahead.”  
     2. Encoder–Decoder Attention  
       – Queries come from the decoder’s previous layer, Keys/Values come from the final encoder layer.  
       – Allows the decoder to attend to source tokens.  
     3. Feed-Forward Network  
   Plus the same residual + layer-norm pattern around each.

4. From Decoder to Output  
   • After the top decoder layer you project the vector for each position to the size of the vocabulary and apply softmax → a probability distribution over next tokens.  
   • At training time you feed in the ground-truth tokens (“teacher forcing”).  
   • At inference you sample or take the argmax, then feed that back in (auto-regressive generation).

5. Why It Works So Well  
   – Self-attention connects any two tokens in a single step, so long-range dependencies are easy.  
   – Multi-head lets the model capture many relationships in parallel.  
   – Residual connections + layer norm ensure stable, deep training.  
   – Position encodings reintroduce order without recurrence.  
   – By stacking layers, the model builds hierarchical representations.

6. Training & Scaling  
   • Train on large corpora with next-token (or masked-token) objectives.  
   • Larger models + more data → better features.  
   • Fine-tuning or prompting steers the pre-trained Transformer to specific tasks.

Summary  
A Transformer transforms a sequence of token embeddings into richer representations via repeated rounds of “every token attends to every other token” (multi-head attention) plus simple feed-forward refinements, all tied together by residual paths and layer normalization. In encoder–decoder setups it first builds a context-aware encoding of the input, then the decoder generates output step by step, attending both to its own past and to the encoder’s output. This architecture turns out to be highly parallelizable and extremely effective at capturing both local and global structure in language.
